questions.q: What is a path?
questions.explain: A path like /home/ada/projects/notes.txt lists every folder from the top down to the file. The last part, notes.txt, is only the file's name.
options: The address of a file: the list of folders you walk through to reach it
The name of a file without its folder
The size of a file on disk

questions.q: Ada uses a Mac. Where is her home folder, usually?
questions.explain: macOS keeps home folders under /Users. Linux uses /home/ada, and Windows uses C:\Users\ada.

questions.q: Which character separates folders in a path on Linux and macOS?
questions.explain: Linux and macOS use /. Windows uses \, but most tools accept / on Windows too.

questions.q: Why does the course focus on the commands used on Linux?
questions.explain: Most servers run Linux. macOS has almost the same commands, and Windows has PowerShell with many of the same names, so the skills carry over.
options: Because Windows cannot run a terminal
Because Linux is the only free operating system
Because most servers on the internet run Linux, so you will use these commands on servers later
Because macOS commands are all different

questions.q: What is the difference between the terminal and the shell?
questions.explain: The terminal is the window. The shell (bash, zsh or PowerShell) is the program in it that understands your commands and runs them.
options: They are two names for exactly the same thing
The terminal is the window you type in; the shell is the program inside it that reads and runs your commands
The shell is the window; the terminal is the program that runs commands
The terminal runs on Linux; the shell runs on Windows

questions.q: Which shell do you usually get by default on each system?
questions.explain: Windows uses PowerShell, macOS uses zsh and most Linux desktops use bash. bash and zsh are close cousins, so the course's commands work the same in both.
options: Windows: bash, macOS: PowerShell, Linux: zsh
Windows: zsh, macOS: bash, Linux: PowerShell
Windows: PowerShell, macOS: zsh, Linux: bash

questions.q: The course writes commands like $ mkdir projects. What is the $?
questions.explain: The prompt (often $, % or >) is printed by the shell when it waits for a command. Type mkdir projects and press Enter.
options: Part of the command, which you must type
The shell's prompt, which shows it is ready; you type only what comes after it
A sign that the command costs money
A sign that the command needs administrator rights

questions.q: What is WSL on Windows?
questions.explain: WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) gives you Linux and bash on Windows. It is optional: everything in the course also works in PowerShell.
options: A required program without which the course does not work
A code editor made by Microsoft
An optional way to get a real Linux terminal with bash on Windows
The Windows name for the ls command

questions.q: You opened a terminal and are not sure which folder you are in. Which command tells you?
questions.explain: pwd ("print working directory") prints the current folder. ls lists what is inside it, which is a different question.

questions.q: You type mkdir projects and press Enter. Nothing is printed. What does that mean?
questions.explain: Most commands are silent on success. When something goes wrong, the shell prints an error message.
options: The command failed without saying why
It worked: most commands print nothing when they succeed
The shell is still waiting, so press <kbd>Enter</kbd> again
The folder exists only until you close the terminal

questions.q:
You are in an empty folder and run these commands. What does the last ls print?
$ touch notes.txt
$ mkdir src
$ touch src/app.js
$ ls
questions.explain: ls lists only the current folder: one file and one folder. app.js is inside src, so you would see it with ls src.

questions.q:
What does cat notes.txt print after these commands?
$ echo "Buy milk" > notes.txt
$ echo "Write report" > notes.txt
$ cat notes.txt
questions.explain: A single > replaces what was in the file. To add a line to the end instead, use >>.
options: Buy milk and then Write report on the next line

questions.q: You want to add a line to the end of notes.txt and keep what is already in it. Which command do you use?
questions.explain: >> appends to the end of the file. > would replace everything in it. touch only creates empty files.

questions.q: You are in ~/projects/task-notes. You run cd .. and then pwd. What folder are you in?
questions.explain: .. means "the folder above this one", so cd .. goes up exactly one level, from task-notes to projects.

questions.q: What does a single . mean in a path, as in code .?
questions.explain: . is the current folder and .. is the folder above. So code . opens the folder you are standing in. Your home folder is ~.

questions.q: How do you see hidden files, whose names start with a dot, in bash?
questions.explain: ls -a ("all") also shows hidden files and the . and .. entries. In PowerShell the same is ls -Force.

questions.q: Which PowerShell command creates an empty file, like touch notes.txt in bash?
questions.explain: PowerShell uses New-Item. mkdir would make a folder called notes.txt, and type prints a file that already exists.

questions.q: In the command ls -a src, what is -a?
questions.explain: ls is the program, -a is an option (arguments starting with - or -- are options or flags) and src is a plain argument: the folder to list.
options: An option (a flag), because it starts with -

questions.q: You type nodee --version and bash says nodee: command not found. What is wrong?
questions.explain: "command not found" means the shell cannot find a program with that name. Here the name has an extra e. Read error messages: they nearly always say exactly what is wrong.
options: Node.js is broken and must be reinstalled
A typing mistake: there is no program called nodee

questions.q: On Linux you made a folder projects. Then cd Projects says No such file or directory. Why?
questions.explain: On Linux and macOS, capital letters matter in names. Run ls to see the real name, or type cd pro and press Tab to let the shell complete it.
options: The folder was deleted when you closed the terminal
Names are case-sensitive: Projects and projects are different names

questions.q: Your web server is running in the terminal and you want to stop it. What do you press?
questions.explain: Ctrl + C stops a running program. Tab completes names, and Up brings back the last command.

questions.q: What does the Tab key do when you have typed cd pro?
questions.explain: Tab completes file and folder names. It saves typing and also avoids spelling mistakes, like a wrong capital letter.
options: It completes the name, for example to cd projects
It brings back the last command
It adds a tab space to the folder name

questions.q: What is a package manager like winget, brew or apt?
questions.explain: A package manager installs programs for you: for example brew install git on macOS or sudo apt install git on Ubuntu.
options: A program that installs other programs with one command
A folder where downloaded files are saved
A code editor with a built-in terminal

questions.q: You just installed a tool, but your open terminal says command not found. What should you try first?
questions.explain: The shell finds commands through the PATH, a list of folders. Installers add their folder to it, but a terminal that was already open keeps its old list.
options: Open a new terminal: the old one still has the old PATH list

questions.q: Which command shows where the node program is on Linux or macOS?
questions.explain: which node prints the path of the program, such as /usr/bin/node. In PowerShell, use Get-Command node. If nothing is found, it is not installed or not on your PATH.

questions.q: A forum post says "just run this sudo command to install Node faster". What is the safe choice?
questions.explain: Commands with sudo or "Run as administrator" can change anything on your computer. Only use the tool's official site or your package manager, and be careful with commands copied from the internet.
options: Run it, because sudo makes installs work better
Run it as administrator on Windows instead
Install only from the official website or your system's package manager
Run it, but close the terminal right after

questions.q: Why should you open the whole project folder in VS Code (for example with code .), not a single file?
questions.explain: With the whole folder open, VS Code sees every file of the project. That is how it can show the file list, find code across files and warn about mistakes.
options: Because VS Code cannot open single files
So the editor knows how the files belong together
So the files are uploaded to GitHub

questions.q: Which devtools tab shows every request a page sends and every answer it gets back?
questions.explain: The Network tab lists requests and responses. The Console tab shows messages from the page's JavaScript and lets you run code.

questions.q: In the devtools Console you type console.log(2 + 3). It shows 5 and then undefined. What is the undefined?
questions.explain: console.log prints 5, but itself returns no value. The Console shows that returned value, undefined. It is not an error.
options: The browser could not do the sum
The console telling you console.log gives back no value; you can ignore it
A second line your code printed

questions.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.explain: Git is the tool that saves commits: snapshots of how every file looked. GitHub is one place to keep those projects online, to back them up and work as a team.
options: They are the same program with two names
GitHub records history on your computer; Git stores it online
Git records a project's history; GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online
Git is for Windows and GitHub is for Linux

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without quotes, 2 + 3 is a sum. .length on a list counts its items: there are two tasks.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toUpperCase() turns every letter into a capital. .length counts the characters: d-e-v-e-l-o-p-e-r is 9.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: + glues texts together exactly as they are, with nothing added in between. Here that builds the Linux path of Ada's projects folder.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .length counts every character, including / and .: src (3) + / (1) + app (3) + . (1) + js (2) = 10.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: split("/") cuts the text at every /, giving the pieces home, ada and projects. Two slashes make three pieces.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pieces are projects, task-notes and notes.txt. Positions start at 0, so the last one is at length - 1: the file name.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: List positions start at 0, so parts[0] is the first piece, projects. There are three pieces in total.

questions.q: Each console.log is like an echo in the shell. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call prints one line, in the order the lines are written. Nothing is replaced: that only happens with > when you write into a file.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: startsWith(".") checks the first character. .gitignore starts with a dot, so it is a hidden file; notes.txt does not.

questions.q: Names are case-sensitive on Linux. What does this print?
questions.explain: === compares exactly, so a capital P makes the texts different. After toLowerCase(), both are projects, so they are equal.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The list has two items. Positions start at 0, so files[1] is the second one, list.txt.

questions.q: Windows uses \ in paths, but in JavaScript text \\ is how you write one backslash. What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside quotes, a backslash starts a special character, so one real backslash is written \\. The printed text has single backslashes, like the Windows path.

questions.q: The first line of code --version is the version. What does this print?
questions.explain: \n is a new line, so split("\n") cuts the text into its lines. Position 0 is the first line, the version.

questions.q: Finish linuxPath so it builds a Linux path from a user name and a file: linuxPath("ada", "notes.txt") should return "/home/ada/notes.txt". Use + to join the texts.
questions.explain: Join the pieces with + and put a / between each folder: "/home/" + user + "/" + file. Forgetting the middle / gives /home/adanotes.txt.

questions.q: Finish macPath: macOS home folders are under /Users. macPath("ada") should return "/Users/ada/projects".
questions.explain: macOS keeps home folders in /Users, not /home. Join "/Users/", the user name and "/projects" with +.

questions.q: Finish fileName so it returns the last part of a path. Hint: path.split("/") gives the pieces, and the last piece is at position length - 1. The program should print app.js and then notes.txt.
questions.explain: Split the path at every /, then take the last piece with parts[parts.length - 1]. Positions start at 0, so parts[parts.length] would be undefined.

questions.q: Finish countFolders so it returns how many names are in a path written like "projects/shopping/archive". Hint: split at / and count the pieces. The program should print 3 and then 1.
questions.explain: path.split("/") gives one piece per name, and .length counts them. A path with no / gives one piece.

questions.q: Print the word developer in capitals, and on the next line the number of letters in it. Use .toUpperCase() and .length. The output must be DEVELOPER and then 9.
questions.explain: word.toUpperCase() gives a new text in capitals, and word.length counts its characters. Print each with its own console.log.
questions.starter:
const word = "developer";
// print the word in capitals, then its length

questions.q: Finish isHidden so it returns true when a file name starts with a dot (a hidden file), otherwise false. Hint: "text".startsWith(".").
questions.explain: Hidden files have names starting with a dot, so name.startsWith(".") is the whole check. ls does not show them, ls -a does.
